newsitem.title: USA: NASD urges court to drop former employee's charges.
newsitem.headline: NASD urges court to drop former employee's charges.

text.p: The National Association of Securities Dealers told a federal court on Tuesday that it is "immune" from a former employee's charges that she was forced to resign because she blew the whistle on the group's allegedly lax enforcement of the municipal bond market.

Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher, lawyers for NASD, in a 30-page brief, urged the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York to dismiss Theresa Carr's $20 million damages lawsuit that she filed against NASD on September 4.
Carr charged that she was pushed out as senior compliance examiner in NASD's district 10 office in New York City because of her aggressive probe of "pay-to-play" in the muni market.
But NASD lawyers said today that Carr's charges are meritless because NASD is protected by "absolute immunity" in its role as a "quasi-prosecutor" in the securities markets.

"Most of plaintiff's claims relate to her belief that NASD did not properly investigate...practices in the municipal finance industry, specifically with respect to payments allegedly made to Armacon Securities, Inc.," the brief says.

"Plaintiff is asserting that NASD misapplied its own rules and failed to fulfill its duties...to enforce compliance with the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board's regulatory scheme," the brief says, referring to the 15-member MSRB, which regulates the $1.3 trillion municipal bond market.
But even assuming that Carr has standing to bring her claims, "it is well-established that the NASD is protected by absolute immunity," the brief says.

NASD is closely supervised by the SEC, the NASD lawyers said. As a result, the courts recognize that quasi-regulatory groups like NASD cannot be sued over decisions to probe or not to probe a particular matter, NASD lawyers said.
